evidence.claim: Most stagecoach, mail, freight and telegraph traffic into the basin came this way until after the Uintah Railway arrived around 1905.
evidence.quote: Most of the stagecoach, mail, freight, and telegraph traffic into the Uinta Basin passed through Ninemile Canyon until after the arrival of the Uintah Railway around 1905.

evidence.claim: The freight trade brought ranches and the settlement of Harper into the canyon. In 1990, BLM designated the road a Scenic Backcountry Byway.
evidence.quote: The freight trade led to the settlement of the canyon itself.

evidence.claim: Harper grew from a stagecoach stop into a scattered string of ranches and buildings, without a formal town site.
evidence.quote: One of the main stagecoach stops developed into a town of sorts. Called Harper, it included a hotel, store, school, and an unofficial post office. It lacked a formal town site, simply taking in a long stretch of scattered ranches and buildings.

evidence.claim: Its precinct reached a population of 130 in 1910, but by the early 1920s Harper was a ghost town.
evidence.quote: The Harper precinct as a whole had a population of 130 at its peak in 1910, but in the early 1920s Harper became a ghost town.

evidence.claim: Schooling outlasted the town's busiest years: the school closed permanently in 1931 and was moved to Wellington in the 1930s.
evidence.quote: This was closed for good in 1931 and moved to Wellington in the 1930s; it later burned.

evidence.claim: A few log dwellings and the old stagecoach stop remain.
evidence.quote: Today, only a few structures remain, including the old stagecoach stop and some other log dwellings.

evidence.claim: The two-story hotel burned in the late 1980s or early 1990s, leaving only its stone foundation.
evidence.quote: The two-story Harper Hotel burned to the ground in the late 1980s or early 1990s; only the stone foundation remains now.

evidence.claim: Most of the town site is private property, requiring permission to explore.
evidence.quote: Most of the town site is on private property, so permission is required to explore the area.

evidence.claim: Iron telegraph poles remain among the canyon's stage stations and settler cabins.
evidence.quote: Iron telegraph poles, stage stations and settler cabins are common sights.

evidence.claim: The Army installed surplus Civil War poles around 1886.
evidence.quote: The army installed steel telegraph poles in the Canyon around 1886, that were American Civil War surplus.

evidence.claim: Their use changed with communications technology: the telegraph line became the basin's telephone line in 1907 and served that role until 1917.
evidence.quote: This telegraph line became the telephone line into the Basin in 1907 and remained until 1917.

evidence.claim: The poles then carried a local line into the 1990s.
evidence.quote: The poles have since served a local line until the 1990s.

evidence.claim: Carved petroglyphs and painted pictographs depict animals and hunting scenes on canyon rock faces.
evidence.quote: Petroglyphs (carvings on rock faces) and pictographs (paintings on rock faces) depict animals, hunting scenes and godlike figures.

evidence.claim: The Fremont grew corn and squash on the canyon floor and built granaries high above it.
evidence.quote: the Fremont practiced agriculture, growing corn and squash along the canyon bottom.

evidence.claim: The Fremont grew corn and squash on the canyon floor and built granaries high above it.
evidence.quote: Researchers have also identified hundreds of pit-houses, rock shelters, and granaries, although only a limited amount of excavation has been carried out. Many of these structures are located high above the canyon floor on cliff ledges, pinnacles, and mesas. They were built by the Fremont

evidence.claim: Their presence here dates to AD 950–1250.
evidence.quote: They were built by the Fremont, whose presence in Ninemile Canyon has been dated at AD 950–1250.

evidence.claim: By the sixteenth century, ancestral Utes were adding their own images; horseback hunting scenes date to the 1800s.
evidence.quote: By the 16th century the ancestral Utes were in the canyon. They added to the rock art already on the walls, but in styles of their own. Many scenes, for example, depict Ute hunters on horseback and date to the 1800s.

evidence.claim: BLM identifies trailheads to rock-art sites and a Fremont village in Cottonwood Canyon beyond Frank's Canyon.
evidence.quote: trailheads to rock art sites and a Fremont Village past Frank's Canyon in Cottonwood canyon.

evidence.claim: The images were carved and painted mainly on weathered sandstone, which is susceptible to erosion accelerated by touching and airborne dust.
evidence.quote: Carved and painted mainly on weathered sandstone panels, the images are susceptible to erosion, which is accelerated by touching and airborne dust.
